nutshell: Occluded person ReID gets much harder when a bounding box contains multiple people ('Multi-Person Ambiguity'), since it's unclear which person is the actual query target. KPR reformulates ReID as a prompt-optional task: a transformer ingests the image plus positive/negative semantic keypoints (marking the target vs. other people) to disambiguate, producing part-based embeddings, and the authors release a new dataset (Occluded PoseTrack-ReID) with the multi-person-occlusion annotations needed to train and evaluate this.
contributions: KPR: the first promptable ReID formulation - a Swin-transformer that fuses image tokens with positive/negative keypoint-prompt tokens *before* encoding ('prompt-aware appearance encoding'), unlike prior pose-guided ReID methods that only use pose information after appearance encoding (e.g. for local pooling); the model is prompt-optional, working with or without a prompt using the same weights.

Occluded PoseTrack-ReID (Occ-PTrack): the first ReID dataset with explicit target disambiguation via keypoints for multi-person occlusions, built from PoseTrack21 (1000/1411 train/test identities, 474/170 videos); also releases pseudo-label keypoint annotations (via PifPaf) for four existing standard ReID benchmarks.

Batch-wise Inter-Person Occlusion (BIPO): a data augmentation that composites another training-batch person onto an image (consistently updating the image, prompt, and human-parsing labels) to synthesize multi-person occlusions during training, since real occluded-ReID training sets rarely contain them - shown in the ablation to be necessary for the model to actually learn to rely on prompts.

MSF (Multi-Stage feature Fusion): a Swin-transformer variant that upsamples and fuses features from every stage to preserve full token resolution throughout, instead of Swin's standard progressive downsampling, improving fine-grained part localization.

Repurposes the same promptable ReID model into KPRTrack, an appearance-only multi-person pose tracker (no motion/spatio-temporal cues) that reaches SOTA HOTA on PoseTrack21, showing the approach transfers beyond single-image retrieval.
deficiencies: On Market-1501 - the paper's own 'easy' holistic (non-occluded) baseline case - KPR is not actually the top performer: SOLIDER alone (96.9/93.9 Rank-1/mAP, Table 1) beats every KPR variant including KPR_SOL with prompt (96.6/93.2), even though KPR uses SOLIDER's own pretrained weights as one of its backbones. This sits awkwardly with the paper's claim in Sec. 4.4 that 'our method emerges as the top performer overall.'

The paper's own analysis (Sec. 4.4) concedes that on Market-1501, Occluded-ReID, and Partial-ReID, multi-person ambiguity is rare so 'prompts are not exploited to their full potential' - and the numbers bear this out: prompt vs. no-prompt gaps on these three benchmarks are often under 2-4 points, meaning most of the paper's strongest evidence for the core promptable-ReID idea comes from a single dataset (Occ-PTrack) that the same authors also constructed.

The keypoint pseudo-labels for the four standard ReID benchmarks rely on an unvalidated heuristic - when multiple skeletons are detected via PifPaf, the one closest to top-center is assumed to be the intended target - with no check against ground truth, so an unknown fraction of the prompt/negative-keypoint supervision on those benchmarks could be systematically wrong, and this risk isn't measured.

On the paper's own flagship Occ-PTrack dataset, the strongest backbone variant (KPR_SOL, Exp. 9 in Table 3) actually underperforms the plain ImageNet-pretrained version (Exp. 8): 90.6/81.2 vs. 92.3/82.3 Rank-1/mAP, attributed to a domain gap between SOLIDER's street-surveillance pretraining and Occ-PTrack's sports footage - meaning the paper's own more 'advanced' backbone loses to the simpler one on the dataset built specifically to showcase the method.
notable: The prompt-optionality robustness study (Fig. 5) shows KPR degrades gracefully and roughly linearly as keypoints are progressively dropped from the prompt, staying above the no-prompt baseline until almost all keypoints are removed - a genuinely useful practical property for real deployments with noisy or partial human/pose-model input, understated relative to how central 'prompt-optional' is to the paper's framing. Separately, KPRTrack's result is notable on its own terms: a tracker using pure frame-to-frame appearance matching (explicitly no motion modeling) still beats motion-aware trackers like Tracktor++ and FairMOT on HOTA - evidence that a sufficiently occlusion-robust ReID embedding alone can substitute for spatio-temporal cues in this benchmark.
